⚡ 1

Voltage Sensor Audit & Power Measurement

Does a voltage column exist in the DCS?

Finding: There is NO VOLTAGE COLUMN in the entire DCS export. Only motor drive current CCRNIIK001AM1.PV (Amperes) is logged.

Electrical load is measured directly via the 3-phase line current. During normal loaded compression, current is rock-steady at 142.4 ± 0.6 A.

⚙️ 2

Duty/Standby Architecture vs Rapid Cycling

Does the compressor cycle between load and unload?

Finding: Centrifugal process gas compressors run in continuous multi-month campaigns, not rapid loading/unloading cycles.

Step-change mathematical audit revealed only 0.014% of 5-min intervals had current shifts > 10 A. Compressor A & B alternate in Duty/Standby mode (Standby: 0.10 A, Duty: 142.5 A).

📐 3

Mathematical Proof: Why Scaling is Not Required

Do we need StandardScaler or MinMaxScaler for Isolation Forest?

Finding: No feature scaling is required. Standard Isolation Forest selects random orthogonal splits along individual single features.

Monotonic transformations preserve order: \(x_a < x_b \iff ext{scale}(x_a) < ext{scale}(x_b)\). Tree depth and partition splits are mathematically identical. Keeping raw units preserves direct operational interpretability.

🚨 4

The Root Cause of the July 2021 Failure

Why was vibration high while output was low?

Finding: Anti-Surge Recycle Valve CCRNHIC0773A.PV was held open at 66.6% for 4 months.

Two-thirds of the gas recycled internally. The motor drew high power (144.4 A) but net forward flow dropped by -8.0σ. High-speed bypass turbulence caused casing vibration to skyrocket to 7.3 mm/s (ISO Zone D Danger).

Regime 2: Healthy Baseline

March 2020 startup: Motor current rose smoothly to 142.5 A. ASV closed (0%). Vibration stable at 3.5 mm/s.

May–August 2021: Anti-surge valve opened to 66.6%. Casing vibration jumped into ISO Zone D Danger (5.5–7.3 mm/s).

Why was it NOT a Bearing Wipe / Mechanical Failure?

If a journal or thrust bearing had wiped, radial shaft vibrations (VI0780A1/A2) and bearing pad temperatures (TI0785A, TXI0790) would have spiked past 85–100°C. In the actual telemetry, bearing metal temperatures stayed completely stable at 54–57°C. The vibration was purely aerodynamic acoustic resonance vibrating the machine casing due to continuous high-velocity bypass recirculation.

Cell-by-Cell Presentation Script for Colleagues

Step-by-step walkthrough to present compressor_anomaly_detection_guide.ipynb to your engineering team.

Slide 1: Ingestion & Telemetry Scope (Cells 1 to 5)

Script: "We are analyzing 214,110 rows of 5-minute supervisory telemetry from Compressor Train A spanning from January 2020 to January 2022. Using the Rust calamine engine, we ingest this 278 MB dataset in under 15 seconds."

Slide 2: Instrumentation & Feature Down-Selection (Cells 6 & 7)

Script: "Refinery instrumentation follows ISA-5.1. Instead of feeding all 71 redundant tags (which dilutes tree splits across 12 stator slots and zero-variance keyphasor tags), we down-selected 15 core indicators covering Power, Flow, Radial Vibration, Casing Vibration, Rotor Thrust Position, and Thermal subsystems."

Slide 3: Regimes & Scaling Myth (Cells 8 to 13)

Script: "Does this machine undergo loading/unloading cycling? No, it operates in campaign duty/standby mode. Furthermore, Isolation Forest does not need feature scaling because tree splits are orthogonal cuts on single features. Standardizing data does not change the tree depth."

Slide 4: Verification & Specificity (Cells 14 to 18)

Script: "Trained strictly on clean March 2020 loaded data, the model achieved 99.44% specificity (only 0.56% false alarm rate on unseen normal operation). In July 2021, it flagged 99.69% of abnormal points with zero false negatives."

Slide 5: Root Cause Diagnosis (Cells 19 to 21)

Script: "When the alarm fired, what broke? Our Z-score attribution ranked the fault drivers: Anti-Surge Valve was held open at 66.6% (+4.8σ), net flow dropped by -8.0σ, and violent bypass turbulence drove casing vibration into ISO Zone D Danger (+6.2σ). Bearing temperatures were normal, proving this was an aerodynamic valve fault, not mechanical wear."
